judge_assessment.explanation: Both hard failures check out, and the first understates the reach slightly. Problem 2 asks the student to "Explain what the calculator actually computed" before giving sin 30 degrees; verify.json id 2 is a single eval expecting 1/2. Problem 3 asks "Name the step Ari skipped"; id 3 is an eval expecting -1/2. Problem 4 asks the student to "State the quadrant of 150 degrees and the sign the tangent must carry there" before the value; id 4 is an eval expecting -sqrt(3)/3, so two of the three requested responses are unchecked. Problem 5 asks the student to "Explain how the size of that answer alone shows the conversion ran the wrong way"; id 5 is an eval expecting 5*pi/4. I would add problem 1, which the judge did not list: "Name the reference angle and the quadrant before you write the value" is two responses beyond the verified -1/2. The second hard failure is exact - problem 7 asks the student to "State how many solutions you expect before solving, and which quadrants they lie in" and id 7 is solve_interval alone, and verify.json contains exactly one manual entry, on id 8. Every exact value the judge recomputed matches my own: -1/2, 1/2, -1/2, -sqrt(3)/3, 5pi/4, 210 and 330 degrees, pi/4 and 7pi/4, and cos 3 = -0.98999 -> -0.99.

strengths_to_preserve: Every planted error is numerically real, not invented: sin(30 radians) genuinely is -0.988, 225 x 180/pi genuinely is 12891.6, and tan 30 degrees genuinely is 0.577. Each is declared as a trap with its value, so the key's Common wrong answers block tells a grader exactly which wrong number means which wrong reasoning.

Problem 5's error is chosen so the wrong answer is absurd on its face - a radian measure of 12891.6 - which lets the sheet ask the student to diagnose from magnitude alone rather than from re-deriving. That is a genuinely well-designed misconception item.

The ASTC quadrant diagram at the top of the worksheet is deliberately value-free ('No values shown - use the angle given in each problem'), so it functions as a shared convention rather than as data belonging to one problem.

Problem 8 is the one correctly handled item and shows the author knew the pattern: parts (a) and (c) are declared manual with a desc naming both readings of the bare 3 and the quadrant reasoning, while part (b)'s cos 3 = -0.99 stays machine-verified.

The study guide's Skill 1 states the two-part rule crisply - 'an exact value is (value of the reference angle) with (the quadrant's sign)' - and its worked example decides the quadrant before looking anything up, which is the ordering the worksheet then drills.

root_causes.description: SKILL.md line 249 tells the author to handle error-analysis 'via the ordinary types - the planted wrong result is checkably wrong and the correction checkably right', and to reserve manual for genuinely open reasoning. On a sheet whose declared instructional_mode is misconception-analysis, that instruction produced exactly what it describes: the corrected values are verified and the diagnoses, which are the point of the sheet, are not recorded at all. The instruction is correct about the correction and silent about the diagnosis.

improvements.title: Require a manual entry whenever a problem asks the student to explain, name or justify
improvements.proposed_change: Rewrite SKILL.md line 249 to separate the two halves of an error-analysis item. The corrected value is checkable and should stay machine-verified; the named diagnosis is a second printed response and must carry its own manual entry whose desc holds the model diagnosis. On a sheet whose instructional_mode is misconception-analysis, make at least one manual entry per diagnostic problem a build requirement rather than a suggestion.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/check_manual_coverage.py plus a fixture whose problem stem contains an explain-class imperative (explain / justify / name the error / say in words / state whether) while its verify.json id has no entry of type manual. The gate must exit non-zero. I ran this exact lint over the ten cases in this shard: it fires on curr-402 (7 ids), curr-406 (4), curr-419 (5), curr-426 (2), curr-438 (5) and curr-450 (3), and stays silent on all three ACCEPTs (curr-413, curr-425, curr-432) - zero false positives. Fails before the fix, passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Problems 1 through 5 and 7 gain manual entries covering the diagnoses, raising the manual count from 1 to 7 and making the exit-2 report describe what the sheet actually asks a human to grade. Removes the hard failure that drove instruction_following to 1.
improvements.risk: Verb-list linting will miss paraphrases ("what does that tell you about ...") and could nag on stems that merely narrate. Keep the list short, allow an explicit per-problem opt-out field in the JSON, and ship at exit 2 first.

improvements.title: Bind verification to every printed answer slot, not to one check per problem id
improvements.proposed_change: Count printed responses per problem. Problem 1 requests three (reference angle, quadrant, value) and verifies one. Problem 4 requests three (quadrant, sign, value) and verifies one. Problem 7 requests three (expected count, quadrants, exact solutions) and verifies one. Reference angle, quadrant and solution count are all machine-checkable given an eval or a count entry, so most of this gap closes without new manual items.
improvements.regression_test: Add a tests/fixtures case with a two-slot problem: the worksheet prints "(a) find the value ... (b) write the rule" under one \problem id while verify.json carries a single entry for that id. A new answer-slot gate must exit non-zero naming the id and the uncovered slot. Today build.sh exits 0 on exactly this shape, so the test fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Six of eight problems gain the missing checks; the reference-angle and quadrant answers become verified rather than assumed, which is the specific reasoning this topic is about.
improvements.risk: Slot counting from prose is heuristic; an over-eager counter could fail well-formed sheets. Mitigate by counting enumerated sub-parts and explicit "write ... on the answer line" phrases only, and by shipping the first release at exit 2 (manual review) rather than exit 1.

improvements.title: Make at least one study-guide try-it rehearse the sheet's declared focus
improvements.proposed_change: check_study_guide.py already enforces structure (two \step lines, a boxed answer, one id per box). Add a coverage assertion: the union of the study guide's try-it skills must include the task's declared focus skill. For a misconception-analysis sheet that means at least one try-it presenting a planted error for the student to name, paired with a manual entry as SKILL.md already permits when the example is also manual.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture study guide whose worksheet focus is 'diagnosing degree-radian errors' but whose three try-its are all plain evaluations. The coverage gate must fail it. Passes today - check_ss_coverage only requires the guide's skills to intersect the worksheet's skill set, which pure evaluation already satisfies.
improvements.expected_impact: The study guide would actually rehearse the graded skill. Applies to every misconception-analysis and concept-models case in the suite, where the guide currently teaches the computation and the worksheet grades the diagnosis.
improvements.risk: Forcing a manual try-it makes more guides exit 2, which could dull the signal of the exit-2 report. Keep the requirement to one try-it per guide.

case_summary: Mathematically flawless and pedagogically well-aimed, but it verifies the wrong half of itself. Every exact value recomputes correctly (-1/2, 1/2, -1/2, -sqrt(3)/3, 5pi/4, {210, 330}, {pi/4, 7pi/4}, cos 3 = -0.99) and every planted error is a real number a real calculator would produce. But this is a misconception-analysis sheet: six of its eight problems ask the student to name or explain what went wrong, and the verification manifest records the corrected values plus one manual entry. Problem 8 shows the author knew how to declare a diagnosis manual and did it well; problems 1 through 5 and 7 did not. The instruction in SKILL.md line 249 is a direct contributor - it tells the author that error-analysis is handled by the ordinary types, which is true of the correction and false of the diagnosis. The study guide repeats the blind spot: all six of its checks are computations, so nothing in the packet rehearses the skill the worksheet grades.
